paragraphs: A motivation worth experiencing is willingness to understand role requirements, compare performance materials, and write every recommendation reason as evidence a director can review; liking film and television or knowing celebrities is not by itself enough to show suitability for casting work.

Experience aesthetic judgment together with organizational work: candidate materials, invitation replies, scheduling changes, and audition records all need accurate maintenance. Liking to evaluate performance also means being willing to handle repeated communication, version updates, and feedback that a candidate was not selected.

Start by choosing a task scenario: role casting focuses on character and performance fit, extras coordination focuses on headcount, schedules, and organization, and talent file maintenance focuses on information accuracy. This page treats these as task directions within the occupation and does not mix agency representation or actor performance into the same responsibility.

Use the fictional candidates and role requirements from the entry module for paper screening, scoring, and scheduling. Do not contact real actors, upload real résumés or audition videos, or promise hiring. The point of the experience is explaining trade-offs, recalculating scores, and recording items that need production-side confirmation.
Are you suited to casting and talent coordination?

Observe whether you can distill criteria from a role description, compare candidates using performance evidence, schedule auditions accurately, and pass consistent information among directors, actors, and agents. Screening conclusions must be explainable, and data permissions and final decision authority must be confirmed first.
This is an editorially designed occupational experience, not a recruitment assessment. A work sample can show screening thinking but cannot replace real project experience or employer requirements.

More specific fit signals are: you are willing to read the role description before looking at candidate materials; you can distinguish missing data from insufficient ability; when describing performance you give observations rather than just saying you liked it; when the director changes requirements you recheck the criteria; and when scheduling auditions you consider availability, materials, contacts, and feedback records. You can also honestly state which information is unverified, and you do not use appearance labels or software scores in place of a complete judgment.

Signals to be cautious about include: only wanting to meet celebrities and not wanting to do data organization; labeling candidates based on personal preference; treating no reply as a rejection; forwarding videos without authorization; or promising candidates a role or pay that you have no authority to decide. Casting is also not an agency finding work for actors, so the role direction and the responsible party should be clarified first.

After the exercise, record: why people excluded by hard requirements were excluded, what makes the shortlisted ones preferred, how scheduling conflicts were handled, and which piece of information still needs confirmation. Then judge whether you are willing to do similar screening and coordination long term.

This page uses the US O*NET-SOC 27-2012.04 Talent Directors as its identity baseline, focusing on auditions, candidate evaluation, and talent coordination. The Chinese name is this page's explanatory rendering and does not prove that a legally named occupation or unified entry qualification exists in China.

First gather the role description, audition materials, production dates, budget range, and candidates' available schedules; list missing conditions as pending confirmation, and do not turn unavailable information into a conclusion that a candidate is unqualified. Real contract requirements are confirmed by authorized personnel.

Separate hard requirements from comparable performance: first check scheduling and task requirements, then use the same materials to observe role understanding, expression, and response to feedback. Scoring is only an editorial exercise tool; real casting should have the project team explain the criteria and trade-offs.

Organize role requirements, candidate materials, and audition records by project to form a reasoned shortlist and a pending-confirmation list. The editorial suggestion is to keep a version and change note with each update, so that directors and liaisons do not use different lists.

After a role requirement or shoot date changes, recheck candidates' availability, material fit, and evaluation criteria; the original score cannot directly prove fit for the new role. Record who confirmed the added conditions and when they take effect.

Casting staff contact actors and agents and submit recommendations to directors and producers, or select personnel as authorized; final selection and contracting authority are defined by the project. Do not write a coordination contact as an actor's agent or legal officer.

The O*NET work context includes frequent phone, email, and face-to-face collaboration; project pace affects liaison and audition scheduling. This page does not treat the parent production occupation's long hours or self-employment share as the precise distribution for the casting sub-occupation.

When delivering candidate lists, audition evaluations, and scheduling status, state the material viewing scope, retention arrangements, and items requiring continued confirmation. The editorial suggestion is to use only fictional data in work samples; public use of real videos or résumés requires separately verified permission.

Casting work can be understood as two task lines, role screening and audition coordination: the former produces a reasoned candidate list, the latter produces executable invitations and records. Both share role conditions, talent data, and information permissions; the following is an editorially organized flow, not a uniform industry procedure.
Role screening and recommendation
Read the role description → clarify conditions → review candidate materials → organize auditions → compare performance → submit recommendations
Candidate shortlist, recommendation reasons, alternatives, and unverified items
Audition coordination and data management
Check availability → contact the actor or agent → send materials → confirm sessions → record feedback → update talent files
Invitation sheet, session scheduling, audition records, and candidate status
Shared professional foundation
Role understanding · evidence comparison · scheduling and liaison · information accuracy · permission confirmation · collaborative judgment
How are casting and actor representation distinguished?

Casting staff are commissioned by the production to find and evaluate performers for roles; actor agents represent actors in seeking work and negotiating. The two may jointly contact candidates, but the commissioning party and interests differ. The table below is based on the US Casting Society's explanation and does not extrapolate to various agency business licenses in China.
Core purpose
Find suitable performers for a production project and make reviewable recommendations based on role needs and audition performance.
Represent actors in seeking work opportunities, coordinate professional business, and negotiate per the agency agreement.
Main object and basis
Script, role description, candidate résumés and performance materials, production schedule, and project authorization.
The actor's representation mandate, career goals, available schedule, and the conditions of the proposed project.
Core process
Analyze the role, contact candidates, organize auditions, compare evidence, submit the list, and coordinate follow-up confirmation.
Seek opportunities per the agency agreement, submit actor materials, communicate about projects, and negotiate cooperation terms.
Main outputs
Role candidate lists, audition records, recommendation opinions, and conditions the production side needs to confirm.
Project opportunities secured for actors, agency business communication, and negotiation results.
Responsible party
Accountable to the production that engages its services; authority over selection and contract negotiation must be defined per project.
Bears agency responsibility toward the commissioning actor; the service scope and fees are checked against applicable law and the agency agreement.

Submit suitable actors to the production or casting team, and handle business communication on the actor's behalf.
Delivery boundary
The CSA states that casting staff do not represent actors and do not charge agency fees to actors they recommend; this statement applies to the role as described by that US professional organization.

Agency business does not equal holding the production's final casting authority; related licensing and fee requirements in China should be checked separately against the actual business and jurisdiction.
Key occupational judgments

Key judgments include whether role conditions are clear, whether candidate materials are reliable, whether evaluation uses the same standard, whether the schedule is executable, and whether recommendation and hiring authority are distinguished. The following is an editorial self-check and cannot treat table scores as the sole basis for real hiring.
Are hard role requirements separated from comparison criteria?
Are the input materials and schedule complete and verifiable?
What must be rechecked after a role or scheduling change?
How is the recommendation list explained to the director?

For each shortlisted person, list role-related observations, conditions met, and information still pending; do not use "felt best" in place of evidence. When the director changes requirements, update the list and explain the changes.
Can candidate materials and audition videos be used this way?

First check the purpose of data collection, who may view it, and the scope of subsequent use; submitting an audition does not automatically equal permission to publish or to train models. Personal information processing in China should be checked separately under applicable rules, and exercises use fictional data only.
What status and permission statements are also needed at delivery?
Requirement analysis | Break down role and talent needs | Read the script and check the required roles, headcount, and conditions with the producer or director to form the screening basis.
Talent search | Review résumés and performance materials | View photos, résumés, videos, and available schedules, and select the people to invite to audition.
Audition organization | Arrange sessions and materials | Provide role and script materials to actors, contact the actor or agent to confirm audition times, and record status.
Evaluation and recommendation | Form candidate and backup lists | Compare role fit and audition performance, and select actors as authorized or submit lists for the producer and director to decide.
Business coordination | Communicate cooperation terms | Coordinate actors, agents, and the production within the defined project authority; contract commitments are confirmed by authorized personnel.
Data maintenance | Update talent and project records | Maintain performers' specialties, experience, and availability information, supervise staff assisting with search, and keep project records.
Section title | The work environment of casting and talent directors

Casting staff work between project requirements, candidate materials, and audition feedback, combining data review, talent judgment, and extensive liaison. The specific organization, hours, and responsibility scope should follow the project role description.

Organization and location | Film, broadcast, or stage projects may hold on-site or remote auditions; daily material review and invitations may also be done in a casting office. O*NET describes US occupational tasks, and it cannot be concluded from it that all roles in China follow the same office pattern.

Materials and tools | Scripts, role descriptions, candidate résumés, headshots, performance clips, audition records, schedule sheets, and talent files form the main inputs. Spreadsheets, email, and scheduling tools are used to organize information; software brands or expensive camera equipment do not constitute a uniform entry qualification.
One list change affects invitations, auditions, and final recommendations, so check the conditions first and then update the related records.

Scheduling and work intensity | Audition deadlines, production schedules, and candidate availability create time constraints. The editorial suggestion is to check both the volume of materials and the liaison burden during the experience; insufficient evidence: this page did not obtain the working-hours distribution for the casting sub-occupation in China and does not fill it in with parent-level statistics.
Notify related people promptly of information changes, and distinguish confirmed, pending, and cancelled statuses.

Review and responsibility chain | Data administrators check files and permissions, casting leads check evaluations and recommendations, and the director or production side determines selection as authorized. A job title cannot substitute for proof of authority; when hiring or fee commitments are needed, first confirm the approving party.

Quality and occupational requirements | Recommendations matching role conditions, accurate candidate materials, executable invitations, substantiated evaluations, and clear material use are the editorially observable delivery qualities. Insisting on verification and records is more useful than showing a large but unexplainable talent list.

How do you choose between tasks within casting and adjacent occupations?

First distinguish role recommendation and audition data coordination within the occupation from adjacent occupations such as agency, teaching, and visual coordination. Shared participation in production does not mean the outputs and commissioning relationships are the same; choose by the tasks you are willing to keep doing and the capabilities you need to build, and do not treat a job title as a directly interchangeable credential.

If you like role requirements and evidence comparison, start with candidate recommendation; if you like data and liaison, first test audition support. When moving toward agency, teaching, or visual coordination, build evidence and requirements according to the target output. One experience only helps narrow the exploration range and does not guarantee hiring or career success.

Tasks within the occupation use the O*NET casting profile; agency, the two teaching roles, and art director each use independent O*NET occupational definitions. The CSA statement distinguishes production commissioning from actor representation. Fit signals are editorial suggestions, and Chinese qualifications and real employer conditions are verified separately.

After choosing a specific direction, then judge which tasks AI changes and which authorization and collaboration responsibilities still require people, and avoid replacing role analysis with industry slogans.

At the technical capability level, editorially testable uses include extracting conditions from a role description, organizing candidate materials, drafting invitations, and detecting scheduling conflicts. Use fictional or approved materials, compare outputs item by item with the original, and record errors and rework; a tool producing a table does not equal accurate understanding of a role, nor does it prove improved real casting quality.

Data organization, audition organization, and candidate recommendation are different tasks. The first can test field extraction, scheduling requires checking times and replies, and recommendation requires explaining role fit; a generated summary cannot be treated as a candidate's real ability or proof of authorization.

Insufficient evidence: this round did not obtain representative AI adoption rates, net time savings, or real casting quality studies for casting 27-2012.04. Tool product capabilities, professional discussions, and contract rules are none of them a national adoption rate; confirming actual adoption also requires project tasks, samples, usage periods, and human rework records.

The responsibility chain starts with clarifying tasks and material permissions, then checking processing conditions, outputs, and logs. The editorial suggestion is to confirm recipients and permitted uses separately for candidate materials and unreleased scripts; real rules apply by region and project contract, and a software interface cannot replace authorization.

A historical SAG-AFTRA self-taped audition notice required secure storage and restricted access, with consent needed for public use. This page uses it to flag audition material boundaries; real projects still check the current agreement version and coverage, and the 2024 notice is not written as a general rule currently in force in all markets.

Before evaluating or recommending, return to the candidate's original materials to check accuracy and distinguish missing data from unmet conditions. The editorial suggestion is not to use software output of appearance, personality, or suitability labels as the sole casting basis; specific personal information processing is checked separately by jurisdiction and permission.

People still bear responsibility for role standards, candidate evaluation, liaison, and final authorization. First verify where a tool helps, then observe whether the work actually changes; when unknown, keep the gap and do not turn technical capability into a wage or job-disappearance ratio.

Insufficient evidence: the net employment change for the casting sub-occupation caused by AI was not obtained. The BLS parent-level producer and director projection includes multiple factors and cannot be separated into an independent AI effect, nor can parent-level growth be extrapolated to casting or Chinese roles. Tasks, adoption, and employment outcomes each need matching evidence.

O*NET lists material review, audition, talent file, and liaison tasks; these can locate the scope of tool experiments, but an occupational profile does not prove that a specific AI tool is effective or has been adopted.
AI's impact on casting work: view organizing, coordination, and judgment separately

AI can serve as a trial tool for data organization, invitation drafts, and schedule checking; whether it is accurate, how much it is actually adopted, and its employment impact are verified separately. The external materials used here supply no measured task-level quantitative score and shows a separate editorial estimate, without an unemployment probability. Role fit and final recommendations require human evidence and clear authority. AI Impact Score 50% is an editorial estimate. Can AI help organize role conditions?

An extraction draft can be tested and checked item by item against the script and role description; when conditions are missed or assumptions added, correct them manually. This is an editorial suggestion and does not claim proven improvement in casting results.
Can a tool score decide who best suits a role?

It cannot decide that directly. You need to know the criteria, inputs, and errors, and explain the trade-offs with actual performance evidence; a model label cannot replace role judgment, project authorization, or information permission.
Does submitting audition material permit publication and model training?

It cannot be presumed in general. Check the collection purpose, recipients, retention, and subsequent use separately; when Chinese law or US agreements apply, handle it per the specific scope, and do not treat the act of submission as permission for all uses.

Can a US audition notice be applied directly to Chinese projects?

It cannot be applied automatically. The notice can indicate material and process checkpoints, but real obligations are judged by region, contract category, version, and specific conduct; keep the original provisions and have the responsible person confirm.

First write the task, material permission, success criteria, and human reviewer; test extraction, ranking, and scheduling with fictional candidates. Record errors, rework, and output use, and an unknown service cannot be treated as a private space.

Material understanding, weighted calculation, and scheduling attention can each be verified separately. In this page's exercise, first flag B as unavailable, then calculate the four people's scores, and finally recalculate the two auditions and the buffer. If you make an error, locate whether it is a misread condition, a multiplication, a sum, or a missed reply, and do not judge overall intelligence from one mistake. A correct calculation only proves performance on this problem, not the ability to serve as a real casting director.

When the director adjusts role conditions, restate the change first, then update the screening and recommendation. E1: role "librarian", with the hard requirement of availability on both D1 and D2. Compare three performances: role understanding 40%, expression 35%, response to feedback 25%, each scored 0—10; the total is the weighted sum of the three, and all exercise data is fictional.

Four people's data: A available both days, 8/7/9; B only on D1, 9/9/8; C available both days, 7/8/8; D available both days, 8/8/7. The three items are in the same order with the same weights; A/C/D materials may be viewed for this exercise, and B does not meet the scheduling requirement.
Your task

E2: first screen by the hard requirements, then calculate the four weighted scores; recommend a primary choice and backup from those who qualify, stating the reasons and the difference from real hiring.

E3: schedule auditions only for the primary choice and backup. Starting at 09:00, 20 minutes per person, with a 10-minute buffer between adjacent sessions, and both are available in that period. List start and end times, the reason for the order, and the invitation status; when no reply is received, write pending confirmation.
Reference answer and recommendation

Weighted scores: A=8×0.40+7×0.35+9×0.25=7.90; B=8.75, but excluded for lacking D2; C=7.60; D=7.75. The qualifying order is A, D, C; primary choice A, backup D. This order holds only under this problem's weights and hard requirements.

No real actors, contact information, or videos are used, and health, personality, and protected attributes are not inferred. description.text: Casting and talent directors find, audition, and evaluate performers for stage, film, or broadcast projects, organizing role requirements, performance evidence, schedules, and production conditions into candidate lists.
